where: target_product_profiles.csv TPP-03 label_and_claims and avoid; ch24.6 Labels; ch29.1 finding 8
current: Honest percentage labelling; value lines first; no imitation claims; avoid 'just like real meat'; ch24.6: avoid nhân tạo (artificial) and anything that sounds like giả (fake)
proposed: Add: avoid độn (padding) and 'x% meat replaced' wording. In press advice, a provincial CDC page and seller claims, độn means hidden cost-cutting (giò độn bột); sellers advertise không độn bột and không độn đạm đậu nành. where: demand_moves.csv DMV-07; ch29.4; ch22 For each reader (research bodies)
current: Chay composition and authenticity survey: measured protein, additives and meat DNA; closes the trust gap and gives makers protein targets
proposed: Re-weight: test borax, preservatives, microbes and protein first, and add animal DNA as a low-cost screen (QUATEST 3 sells real-time PCR for 86 species at 0.001% since February 2025). The 2015 to 2026 record has no confirmed case of meat in chay but repeated borax, botulism and unlabelled-origin cases. Publish with VFA, publish methods and do not name small makers: the 2016 Vinastas fish-sauce survey (101 of 150+ samples flagged) led to delistings, a Ministry of Health rebuttal and a backlash against the testers.

where: ch22.4 Trust is the weakest point
current: A Can Tho University team built a DNA test for meat in vegetarian food, citing many cases of meat found in chay foods; we found no survey of how often this happens
proposed: Add: we also found no press or official report confirming meat in a Vietnamese chay product in 2015 to 2026. The only official case is an April 2021 seizure of more than 3 t of chả đòn chay in An Giang on suspicion of meat and fish, with no published result. Meat-in-chay stories circulate as a relayed Taiwanese scandal (2015) and social-media videos; the press record on chay is about borax, microbes and unlabelled goods.

current: Numeric protein claim (giàu đạm); short ingredient list; traceable origin and verified meat-free status
proposed: Add: fake chay is a latent rumour, not a live scandal, so it does not weaken a protein claim now. Chay's live trust problems are safety and additives; the protein claim is credible when it rides on a registered maker, a full label and a short additive list. Keep 'verified meat-free' as a secondary reassurance, bought as a PCR screen.

current: W8-L1: largely in force; narrow to generic names: a voluntary industry code to state the meat share when a plant or fungal protein replaces 10% or more of the meat
proposed: Add to rationale: declared percentages are enforced criminally (2017 beef balls labelled 70% or more beef, pork DNA only). The fraud frame lives in unlabelled market giò and exempt small businesses, which a label rule does not reach. The code's value is defensive: proof against a độn accusation.

current: The Vietnamese press uses thịt nhân tạo for cultivated meat ...; thịt giả (fake meat) is a crime story in Vietnam
proposed: Add: the same outlet uses thịt giả for both; 6 of Dan Tri's first 11 results for the term are about plant-based or cultivated meat and 4 about fraud; a 2020 headline warned that soy pork in restaurants could be a cú lừa (a trick).
